You understand and use the colloquial register of spoken Spanish at B2 level: interjections and filler words (pues, venga, vaya, anda, hombre, o sea, bueno), intensifiers (súper, mogollón, un montón, qué pasada, de miedo), reaction phrases (¡no me digas!, ¡qué fuerte!, ¡ni de broma!) and you know when NOT to use them (formal register).

To distinguish colloquial from formal register and choose well: you don't write "mola mogollón" in an official letter.
Sunday on the Cuesta de Moyano
Sunday, 14 March, at Lucas's book stall on the Cuesta de Moyano. Costel has brought a load to Madrid and is staying with Andrei. Lucas is from Cádiz and speaks very colloquially.
Hey, Costel! At last! Andrei's told me loads about you.
Nice to meet you. Well… is this Faustino's stall?
It was. Now it's mine, for one euro. What do you think? Cool, eh?
Very cool. And you open it every Sunday?
Every single one, mate. I promised Faustino. No way I'd close it on a Sunday.
Costel came by truck from Bucharest. Four days.
You don't say! No way! So you crossed half of Europe with twenty tonnes?
Twenty-two. And speaking Spanish at every petrol station.
Well, well. You speak better than my cousin from Jerez. Amazing!
Oh, come off it. You're only saying that to sell me a book.
"ni de broma" = no way, not even as a joke
In fast speech, "pues" is reduced: "pos" or just "pue". In Andalusia final "s" often disappears: "pue sí". Recognise it, but say "pues" clearly yourself.
Colloquially, "para" becomes "pa": "pa' casa", "pa' ti". And participles in -ado lose the "d": "cansao", "pasao". Don't write them like that in formal texts.
With rising intonation = "come on!" (encouragement); falling and short = "OK, deal"; repeated ("venga, venga") = hurrying or disbelief.
1. The words that keep a conversation going
Es que se lo prometí a Faustino.
These words aren't translated word for word. Without them, your Spanish sounds correct but "textbook". With too many, it sounds forced. One per sentence is enough.
Come on, you can do it! (encouragement)
Oh no! I've forgotten my phone. (annoyance)
Oh, come off it, I don't believe you. (disbelief)
The meaning depends on intonation and context. Listen for them in Spanish films and series: they're everywhere.
to be cool, to be blown away, to work
"Tío / tía" (mate, girl) is used only among friends, especially young ones. Don't call your boss or an older stranger "tío".
Me gusta mucho. / Resulta muy interesante.
In the DELE B2, the oral exam accepts a relaxed tone, but in the written exam (formal letter, article) colloquialisms lower your mark. Adapt to the person you're addressing.

On 1 March, in Romania, people give each other mărțișoare: small ornaments tied with a white and red string, worn pinned to clothing all month to bring luck and health. Rosa Elena had been preparing them for weeks at the Spanish club. She had persuaded Mrs Ionescu that this year the club children had to make mărțișoare not just for their mothers, but also for Spain. They made nineteen. Each one came with a card in Spanish explaining the tradition, written by the children in the clearest handwriting they could manage. Ana sent them by express post on 20 February, in a padded envelope, to the bookshop in Triana.

Ecaterina handed them out on 1 March, still in Triana, a week before going back to Bucharest. She pinned one on doña Remedios's cardigan, a four-leaf clover painted green. She pinned another on Faustino's lapel, next to his beret: a little wooden lamp. Curro got a tiny guitar. And she put the rest in envelopes and sent them to Madrid: for Marta, for Lola, for Lucas, for Andrei, for Begoña and for Inés. Each envelope contained the children's card. Doña Remedios read hers aloud at breakfast, slowly, with her glasses on the tip of her nose. When she finished, she said that from that year on there would be mărțișoare in Triana too.

In Madrid, the most unexpected reaction was Begoña's. Andrei left the envelope on her desk one Monday morning and went to his place without saying anything. Begoña opened it, took out the mărțișor, a little camera made of black felt with the white and red string, and read the card. Andrei watched her out of the corner of his eye from the darkroom. Begoña looked at the little camera for a while. Then, without saying anything, she pinned it to her jumper, over her heart. She wore it all month. When anyone at the agency asked her what it was, she just answered: "A present from a six-year-old photographer. One of the good ones."

Lucas, on the other hand, reacted the way he always did, like a true gaditano. He opened the envelope at the stall on the Cuesta de Moyano on Sunday morning, in front of the customers, and shouted: "Look! How cool!" His mărțișor was a tiny cardboard book with blank pages. Lucas hung it round his neck on its string, like a medal, and told all his customers that Sunday about the Romanian tradition, although he told it his own way, adding details that weren't on the card. By mid-morning, according to his version, in Romania the mărțișor helped you win the lottery, find a girlfriend and pass exams. Andrei told him he was making it up. Lucas answered: "Well, a little bit."

Ecaterina returned to Bucharest on Sunday, 7 March. Ana, Rosa Elena and Mr Dan were waiting for her at the airport. The girl had a new sign, written in Spanish in orange marker: "Welcome, Grandma. Is the orange tree in blossom yet?" Ecaterina hugged her so hard that the sign got crumpled. In her suitcase she was carrying the introduction, written out neatly, in a blue folder; a bag of dried orange blossom that doña Remedios had prepared so that the house would smell of Triana for a few days; and a letter from Faustino for Grandpa Gheorghe, in Spanish, which Ecaterina would have to translate for him in person. Faustino had warned her it was confidential. Ecaterina had promised not to read it ahead of time.

That same evening she read the introduction to Ana, in the kitchen, with tea in front of them, as she had promised on the phone. Ana listened without interrupting. When Ecaterina reached the boy from Teruel, Ana covered her mouth with her hand. At the end she stayed silent for a while. Then she said just one thing, in Spanish, the first thing that came to her: "Madre mía." Ecaterina laughed. She told her that was exactly what everyone had said: doña Remedios, Faustino, the neighbour opposite. Ana told her it was because there was nothing else to say. That when something was very good, people stopped talking like books and started talking like the street.

Ecaterina sent the introduction to Inés on Monday, 15 March, after letting it rest another week in the folder, as doña Remedios had advised. The reply came in two parts. The first, that same afternoon, was a text message: "Oh my God, Ecaterina! I've just read the intro. It's amazing. The bit about the boy from Teruel blew me away. Call me when you can, OK? Kisses." The second arrived two days later, by email, with the publisher's logo: "Dear Ecaterina: I can confirm that we have received the introduction. The editorial committee considers it excellent and proposes no changes. Please let us know whether you agree with the planned publication date, 23 April."

Ecaterina showed the two messages to Mr Dan's retired students the following Tuesday, because Mr Dan had asked her to come and talk to them one day. She put them side by side on the board. She asked them if they saw the difference. The former Tarom pilot raised his hand and said that in the first one Inés was talking like a friend, and in the second like a publishing house. Ecaterina told him: exactly. That both messages said the same thing, that the introduction was good, but one said it from the heart and the other with a tie on. The pianist asked which one was correct. Ecaterina answered: both, each in its place.

That class changed something in Mr Dan's group. From then on, the students began bringing colloquial expressions they heard in Spanish series every Tuesday, and Mr Dan, who couldn't help himself, made a table with three columns: "street", "office" and "never in front of a judge". The former Tarom pilot learned "mola" and used it that very week with the receptionist at the Instituto Cervantes, who laughed for five minutes. The pianist learned "¡qué fuerte!" and said it every time someone arrived late. And the three men from the tractor factory discovered "currar", and said it was the first Spanish word they truly understood, with their whole bodies.

At the Friday Spanish club, the effect was similar, though more dangerous. Rosa Elena heard her mother say "¡madre mía!" when she read the introduction and adopted it at once. Then she learned "¡qué pasada!" from one of Andrei's videos, and "tío" from a cartoon series. The following Monday, in maths, when Mrs Ionescu explained an addition with carrying, Rosa Elena raised her hand and said out loud: "¡Qué pasada, tío!" The whole class laughed. Mrs Ionescu didn't. That Friday, at the club, she spent a whole hour explaining the difference between street Spanish and school Spanish. And she banned "tío" until further notice.

Meanwhile, Costel had received some unexpected news. The head of the company called him into his office one Monday and told him there was a problem with that fortnight's Valencia run: the client in Requena had postponed the order. But there was another urgent load, furniture again, for a big shop in Madrid, in the Salamanca district. He asked him whether he would mind changing destination for once. It took Costel a second to answer. Madrid. The city of don Andrés, of La Lámpara, of Lola, of Andrei. He told the boss he didn't mind at all. The boss told him that, judging by his face, anyone would think he'd won the lottery.

He arrived in Madrid on Friday the 12th in the afternoon, after four days on the road. He unloaded the furniture in the Salamanca district and left the truck in a truck park on the outskirts, because with twenty-two tonnes it was impossible to get into the centre. Andrei came to fetch him by metro. It was the first time they had seen each other since Christmas. Andrei was wearing Rosa Elena's mărțișor pinned to his jacket: a little red lamp. Costel asked him if he could stay at his flat until Monday. Andrei told him of course, that he had already made up the sofa, and that on Sunday he had a surprise for him. Costel asked him what surprise. Andrei told him: the Cuesta de Moyano.

On Saturday they went to La Lámpara. Costel stood for a long time in front of the green sign, which he had already seen in photos a hundred times, and in front of the bronze plaque, which he read aloud, slowly, word by word. Then they went in. Lola hugged him as if she had known him all her life, because, as she said, she did: Ecaterina had talked about him so much that he was already family. She showed him the back shelf, under the lamp, with the two books, the Spanish and the Romanian, and the boxes of readers' letters. Costel asked if he could sit for a moment at the back table. Lola told him that table had been reserved for three years for people like him.

Costel sat down. Lola brought him a coffee and a piece of tortilla without asking. Andrei sat opposite. For a while they didn't talk. Costel looked at the lamp, lit although it was daytime, and thought of don Andrés, of the afternoon he had given him the atlas, of the viewpoint, of the stone bench. Then he told Andrei, quietly, that the place was smaller than he had imagined. Andrei told him everyone said the same. That La Lámpara was small on the outside and huge on the inside. Costel nodded. He said it was like Grandpa Gheorghe: a small old man with a heart that could hold half the world.

On Saturday evening, Lucas took them to a tapas bar in La Latina which was, according to him, the only place in Madrid where people talked like in Cádiz. There Costel discovered that colloquial Spanish had more layers than he had imagined. Lucas kept greeting him with "¡quillo!", which according to him was like saying "chiquillo" but in a hurry. The waiter asked him "¿qué te pongo, jefe?", although Costel wasn't anybody's boss. And a lady at the next table, on hearing that he had come from Romania by truck, said to him "¡olé tus narices!", which Costel didn't understand at all. Andrei explained that it was a compliment. Costel wrote it down on a napkin, for Ana.

On Sunday morning they went to the Cuesta de Moyano. It was a bright March day, the kind that in Madrid announces spring ahead of time. The wooden stalls were open, with the books arranged on the shelves and people strolling up the slope, slowly, stopping to browse. Lucas's was the last one, the one that had been Faustino's. Lucas was sitting on the stool, with his tiny-book mărțișor hanging round his neck, arguing with a customer over the price of a Galdós novel. When he saw Andrei arrive with a big man of about sixty, he left the customer in mid-sentence and got up shouting: "Hey, Costel! At last!"

Costel had never heard anyone talk like Lucas. He spoke fast, swallowed half the letters, said "tío" every three sentences and used words that weren't in any of Ana's books: "mogollón", "mola", "flipar", "currar". At first Costel understood half. But after ten minutes he began to catch his rhythm, as when he got used to a new road. Lucas told him the stall was now his, for one euro, and asked him if he thought it was cool. Costel told him he thought it was very cool. Lucas burst out laughing. He told him that a Romanian who said "mola" after ten minutes with a gaditano deserved a prize, and gave him a book.

The book was a dictionary of colloquial Spanish from the nineties, with its covers coming unstuck. Lucas told him he kept it under the counter for foreign customers who didn't understand him. That he was giving it to him because, if he was going to Valencia every two weeks, he'd better learn to talk like people, and not like radio presenters. Costel leafed through it. He found "mogollón", "pasada", "flipar", "molar". And he found a word he didn't know: "currante". Lucas explained that it was a person who worked hard, who gave their all at work. He told him that word was for him. Costel wrote it on the first page, in his big handwriting.

They stayed at the stall all morning. Costel helped Lucas arrange books, take money, wrap. He talked to the customers. An elderly gentleman asked him where he was from, and when Costel told him Romania, the gentleman replied: "Well! No way! You speak better than my grandson." A young woman asked him if he had any Romanian poetry in translation. Costel didn't know. Lucas looked in a box and found a book by Eminescu in Spanish, old and yellowed. The young woman bought it. Costel told her, in Spanish, that he was Romania's most important poet and that his grandmother knew some of his poems by heart. The young woman thanked him and said: "Mola."

At midday Marta turned up, wearing sunglasses and carrying a bag of churros from the San Ginés chocolate shop. She had Rosa Elena's mărțișor on her lapel, a little wooden pencil. She hugged Costel and told him he looked very well, that the truck suited him. The four of them sat on the pavement next to the stall to eat the churros. Marta told them "La librera de Triana" was coming out on 23 April, the same day as Ecaterina's anthology, because Inés had decided the two books were sisters and had to be born together. Lucas said that was amazing. Marta told him yes, it was amazing, but she was scared to death.

Costel asked her why she was scared. Marta explained that this was the first novel she had written about real people, and she was afraid that Faustino and doña Remedios wouldn't recognise themselves, or worse, that they would recognise themselves too much. Lucas told her not to be silly, that Faustino had read the whole novel aloud in the doorway of his bookshop, five evenings in a row, in front of all of Triana, and that, according to Curro, at the end he had said that the Faustino in the novel was a better person than him. Marta took off her sunglasses. She knew nothing about the readings. She was silent. Then she said, very quietly, just one word: "Seriously?" Lucas told her: "Seriously, girl."

In the afternoon, Andrei took Costel to the agency. It was Sunday and it was empty, but Andrei had had a key for a year. He showed him the darkroom, the trays, the red light. And he showed him, hanging from a string with pegs, the three photos that had survived from the film in don Andrés's Zenit: the freshly painted green sign, the paella with the two glasses of wine, and the sea seen from the viewpoint, with the stone wall in the foreground. Costel stood for a long time in front of the third. It was the same sea he had seen in January, from the same spot, forty-odd years later. He said the wall was the same. That not a single stone had changed.

At that moment the agency door opened. It was Begoña. She was wearing a long coat, the big camera over her shoulder and the little black felt camera pinned to her jumper. Andrei froze: Begoña never came to the agency on Sundays. Begoña looked at the two of them, looked at the photos hanging from the string and said, without saying hello, that she had forgotten something in her office. Then she went over to the photo of the sea. She looked at it for a long time. She asked Costel if he was the trucker from the viewpoint. Costel told her yes. Begoña nodded. She told him Andrei had shown her the photo of the empty bench he had taken in January. And that it wasn't bad.

Andrei couldn't believe it. In eighteen months, Begoña had told him "not bad" three times, and now she was saying it to a Romanian trucker who had taken a photo with his phone. Begoña, as if she had read his mind, added that a photo wasn't good because of the camera, but because of the reason it was taken. And that the photo of the empty bench had been taken for the best reason in the world: so that someone who couldn't be there, was. Then she went into her office, came out with an envelope she had forgotten, said goodbye with a gesture and left. Lucas, when Andrei told him that evening, said a single word: "Mind-blowing."

That night, on Andrei's sofa, before opening the dictionary, Costel called Ecaterina. He told her about the visit to La Lámpara, the morning at the stall, Marta's churros and Begoña's appearance at the agency. Ecaterina laughed a lot about Begoña. She told him Begoña had never once said "not bad" to her. Costel asked her if she was going to Madrid on 23 April, for the birth of the two sister books. Ecaterina answered of course, that she wouldn't miss it for anything — "ni de broma". Costel was quiet for a moment. Then he told her she had just said "ni de broma". Ecaterina replied: "Well, of course. I've spent half my life among Spaniards, Costel. Something rubs off."

On Monday morning, before going back to the truck, Costel stopped by La Lámpara again. He wanted to leave something for Lola. It was Lucas's dictionary of colloquial Spanish, which he had read from cover to cover the night before on Andrei's sofa, until three in the morning. On the first page, under "currante", he had written another word in his big handwriting, in Romanian, with its translation: "dor: echar de menos algo o a alguien con todo el cuerpo, y que te guste un poco echarlo de menos." Lola asked him why he was leaving it with her. Costel told her it was because that word was missing from the dictionary, and La Lámpara was the only place in Madrid where everyone understood it without translation.

Meanwhile, in the village, Grandpa Gheorghe received Faustino's letter. Ecaterina went to take it to him on Saturday, 20 March, with Ana and Rosa Elena, and translated it for him on the porch, under the walnut tree, which had no leaves yet but already had its first buds, small and green. The letter was short. Faustino told him the orange tree had blossomed in Triana and that the smell of the blossom reminded him of the walnut tree's walnuts, he didn't know why, perhaps because both smelled of home. He told him he was learning a Romanian game that Curro had shown him online, and that he was practising for the summer. And he asked him whether he could come back in August.

Grandpa listened to the translation in silence. When it was over, he asked Ecaterina to write the reply in Spanish, word for word, as he dictated it. Ecaterina took out her notebook. Grandpa dictated slowly, in Romanian, and Ecaterina translated sentence by sentence. He told Faustino that of course he could come back, that the walnut tree was waiting for him, and that this time he would beat him at mus. He told him that the Romanian game he was learning was probably table, backgammon, and that nobody had beaten him at table since 1962. And at the end, he asked Ecaterina to write one sentence exactly as he said it, without translating. Ecaterina wrote it: "Venga, Faustino. Hasta agosto." Grandpa had learned "venga" from Rosa Elena.

Rosa Elena, who had been listening to everything sitting on the porch step, raised her hand as at school. She said "venga" had many meanings and Grandpa had to be careful. She explained to them, very seriously, that "venga" could mean "come on", or "OK", or "hurry up", or "bye", depending on how you said it. That Mrs Ionescu had explained it to her at the club, with examples. Grandpa asked her what it meant the way he had said it. Rosa Elena thought for a moment. Then she said that, the way he had said it, it meant everything at once: come on, OK, hurry up and bye. And that only grandpas knew how to say it like that. Ecaterina wrote it in the margin of the letter.

On Thursday, 25 March, Costel made his sixth trip to Valencia, this time to Requena again, because the client had now received the postponed order. He arrived at Álex's school on Friday morning, before lessons, as always, to take the photo of the walnut tree's patch. Álex was waiting for him at the garden entrance, hands in his pockets, with a smile he couldn't hide. He didn't say anything. He just pointed at the ground, next to the stake with the green sign. Costel crouched down. In the dark earth, still very small, almost invisible, there was a shoot. A thin stem, as thick as a needle, with two crinkled little leaves at the tip.

Costel said nothing for a long while. He stayed crouched, looking at that shoot, with his knees in the damp earth. Álex crouched beside him. He told him he had seen it on Wednesday, but hadn't told anyone, not even his mother, because he wanted his grandpa to be the first to see it. Costel asked him if the biology teacher knew. Álex told him yes, that she had jumped for joy like a little girl, and had said it was, of the three walnuts, the one he had planted, the biggest one. Costel took out his phone. His hands were shaking so much he had to take the photo three times. Then he called Ana, so she could take the phone to Grandpa.

That same morning, Álex created a message group with his whole class and the biology teacher. He called it "The walnut gang". He made the shoot photo the group picture, and as the first message he wrote, in the Spanish of a fifteen-year-old: "Guys, it's come up. My grandpa's grandpa's walnut tree, I mean Grandpa Gheorghe's, who isn't my grandpa, but it's cool anyway. It needs watering. Come on, rota." Within ten minutes there were twenty-three replies. They organised a watering rota for the whole school year, including the Easter holidays. The biology teacher wrote a single message at the end: "I'm blown away by you lot." Irina took a screenshot and sent it to Ana.

That afternoon, at seven, in the village, Ana put the phone in front of Grandpa on the kitchen table, next to the freshly lit oil lamp. On the screen was the photo of the shoot, enlarged as much as possible. Grandpa put on his glasses. He looked at the photo for a long time, very close, his nose almost touching the screen. Ana thought he was going to say something solemn, one of his sayings, something to write down in a notebook. But Grandpa didn't say anything solemn. He took off his glasses, wiped his eyes on his shirt sleeve and said, in Spanish, with the word he had learned that month from a trucker who had learned it from a gaditano: "¡Qué pasada!"
"de reojo" = out of the corner of the eye
"pillarle el ritmo" = to catch someone's rhythm
"dejarse la piel" = to give one's all
